However, they must end in a legal position and not Within the Engagement Range of any enemy model. Models using the PLACE effect during the Assault Phase may be set Within the Engagement Range of Enemy models (the Unit becomes Engaged).
After rolling to Hit, move up to X failed Attack Dice directly into the Armour Pool. Treat them as successful Hits for all purposes, including Surge.

The default state of a Tactical Card or Faction Card. A Ready card is face-up, its abilities are available, and it may be Exhausted to pay resource costs or activate its Special Abilities. All Tactical Cards and Faction Cards begin each Round in the Ready state. Cards that have been Exhausted are returned to Ready during Cleanup & Refresh (Part 8.9.5).
This ability is exempt from the Once Per Round limit (Part 2.7.1). It may be used multiple times per Round and per Activation, provided all Costs and trigger conditions are met each time.

A holding area off the battlefield where Units remain until they are deployed. All Units begin the game in Reserves. While in Reserves, a Unit: X Cannot be targeted by attacks or abilities unless an ability explicitly states it affects Units in Reserves. X Cannot use Active Abilities, Passive Abilities, or Reaction Abilities unless the ability explicitly states otherwise. X Cannot Control or Contest Mission Markers. X Does not contribute its Current Supply Value to the player’s Total Current Supply on the battlefield. X Retains all equipment, upgrades, and weapon selections assigned during Army Building. X A Unit leaves Reserves when it is deployed to the battlefield via a Deploy action (Part 8.5.5). Some rules may return a Unit to Reserves during play – see Part 8.5.5 for how Damage, effects, and Supply are handled. In the final Round of the game, all Units still in Reserves that are not deployed are treated as Destroyed for scoring purposes (Part 8.10).

Return up to X Destroyed models to this Unit. X The return cannot increase the Unit’s Current Supply Value. Do not return a model if doing so would push the Unit into a higher Supply bracket. X Set each returned model in Base-to-Base contact with an existing model in the Unit. Returned models cannot be set Within the Engagement Range of any Enemy Unit. X If a model cannot be set legally, it cannot be returned.

If a Shield value is present on a Unit Card, add it to the Hit Points (HP) of the first model. The Unit is Shielded. The Unit loses its Shielded Status when the Total Damage assigned to it exceeds its Shield value or when the first model in the Unit is removed. The Shielded Status is referenced by other abilities. Losing Shielded Status does not remove any remaining Hit Points, it only ends effects that require the Unit to be Shielded. Shielded Status cannot be restored by HEAL.

When this Unit performs a Ranged Attack or Close Combat Attack, models equipped with this weapon may use it, ignoring the normal restriction of one weapon per model (Part 8.7.3). If a model is equipped with multiple SIDEARM weapons, it may use all of them in the same activation. Attacks made with each SIDEARM must be resolved in separate Batches. Because they are separate Batches, SIDEARM attacks may target a different Enemy Unit than the Unit’s other weapons, subject to all standard target eligibility requirements.

While a Unit has the SIEGE MODE Status, apply the following rules: X This Unit cannot perform the Move, Disengage, Run, Charge or Close Ranks actions. X Weapons profile with Siege Mode Status can only be used while this unit has SIEGE MODE Status. X While this unit has Siege Mode Status any other weapons can’t be used. X When this Unit is returned to Reserves, it loses the SIEGE MODE Status.

A Special Ability is any named ability printed on a Unit Card, Tactical Card, or Faction Card. Every Special Ability falls into one of three categories: Active Ability, Passive Ability, or Reaction Ability (Part 2.7). X Active Abilities require the Unit to be Activated and are triggered immediately before or after an action. Each named Active Ability may be used once per Round per Unit unless it has the REPEATABLE keyword. X Passive Abilities are always in effect as long as the Unit is on the battlefield. X Reaction Abilities fire in response to a specific trigger. Each player may resolve only one Reaction per Activation, and each named Reaction Ability may be used only once per Round per Unit. All three types are inactive while the Unit is in Reserves unless the ability explicitly states otherwise. A Unit cannot be affected by multiple instances of the same- named Special Ability simultaneously.
A Unit may include only one model equipped with this weapon. Multiple upgrades configuring more than one instance of this weapon are not permitted (Part 9.1.7).

Additional hits generated by a Template Weapon that strike models outside the Primary target Unit. When a Blast Template (BT) or Flamer Template (FT) covers models belonging to Units other than the Primary target, those models are resolved as Spillover. Each affected Unit is resolved as a separate Batch. Spillover Batches do not apply Rate of Attack modifiers and do not generate Surge. Spillover may affect both Friendly and Enemy Units. See Part 8.7.6 for the full Template Weapon procedure.
At the Start of the Round, all Units gain this Status. A Unit immediately loses this Status if any model in this Unit moves, is moved, or is PLACED for any reason.

A category of keyword representing a temporary or persistent operational mode, condition, or statistic modifier affecting a Unit (e.g. BURROWED, SIEGE MODE). Unless stated otherwise, Statuses aren’t removed during the Scoring and Cleanup Phase. They stay on the Unit until they are removed by other means A Unit’s active Status is visually tracked using Status Markers set next to the Unit: X Modes: Use Plastic Markers to track operational shifts (e.g. SIEGE MODE, BURROWED). Those Status Markers have STAY IN PLAY. X Other Statuses: Use Markers to track other effects affecting the Unit. Positive effects are tracked with Buff Markers (Blue), and negative effects are tracked with Debuff Markers (Red). Those Status Markers have STAY IN PLAY.
This Token, Marker or Ability Effect persists through Cleanup & Refresh (overrides Part 8.9.5). It remains until a specific condition removes it (e.g. destroyed or duration expires).

Set the Leading Model of the named Unit in Base-to-Base contact with the Parent Unit. Set remaining models In Coherency. Models cannot be set Within the Engagement Range of any Enemy Unit. Set an Activation Marker next to the summoned Unit – it cannot be Activated during the Phase in which it was summoned. In subsequent Phases, this Unit must be Activated immediately after its Parent Unit’s activation ends, before the opponent’s next activation. The Summoned Unit cannot be set Within the opponent’s Zone of Influence. The player must have sufficient Available Supply. If the Unit’s Current Supply Value would cause Total Current Supply to exceed the Supply Pool, it cannot be Summoned. If the Parent is not present on the battlefield, this Unit can be Activated normally.

The Supply Value of a Unit is the value shown on the Unit Card’s Supply Profile corresponding to the Unit’s current model count. A Unit’s starting Supply Value is determined during Army Building by the Composition Option selected (Part 9.1.6) and defines how many Army Slots the Unit occupies. Supply Value is a dynamic characteristic – as casualties reduce the model count into a lower bracket on the Supply Profile, the Supply Value decreases. Update immediately when a casualty moves the Unit into a lower bracket. Supply is used for Deployment, Mission Marker Control, Tactical Mass, and scoring.

A model is in the Supporting Rank if it is in Base-to- Base contact with a Friendly model from the same Unit that is in the Fighting Rank, but is not itself Within the Engagement Range of an Enemy model. Models in the Supporting Rank may strike with their Combat Phase weapons as though they were in the fight. See Part 8.8.1, Step 2.

A Unit has Tactical Mass when its Current Supply Value exceeds the Combined Current Supply Value of all Enemy Units it is Engaged with. A Unit with Tactical Mass ignores the Disengage penalty (Part 8.5.4): it may Ranged Attack and Charge normally in the following Assault Phase after Disengaging.
When this Unit resolves an Armour Roll, change up to X failed results into successes. Treat them as meeting or exceeding the Armour characteristic – discard them without moving to the Damage Pool.

A Ground Unit is Unengaged when none of its models is Within 1” of any Enemy Ground model, or when terrain restrictions (Part 7.2.1) prevent valid Engagement despite proximity. Flying Units are always Unengaged. An Unengaged Unit may perform a standard Move, Run, Ranged Attack, or Charge without restriction. Only Unengaged Units may be selected to perform a Move action (Part 8.5.2).

A model is Visible to another model if a valid Line of Sight trace can be drawn between them (Part 7.1). If the trace does not pass through any Blocking Terrain, the target is Visible without further checks. If the trace passes through Blocking Terrain, apply the Cover rules (Part 7.1.1) – the target remains Visible unless Full Cover or Direct Cover blocks the Line of Sight. A model with the HIDDEN keyword is not Visible to any model more than 4” away, regardless of Line of Sight.

A model is Wholly Within a distance only if its entire base sits inside that range - no part of the base may extend beyond the edge. A Unit is Wholly Within a distance only if every model in the Unit satisfies this condition. Wholly Within is a stricter requirement than Within and is used for Coherency checks (Part 4.4), certain ability areas of effect, and Mission Marker eligibility. When a rule specifies Wholly Within, partial overlap is not sufficient.

A model is Within a distance if any part of its base touches or crosses into that range. A Unit is Within a distance if at least one model in the Unit meets this condition. Within is a less restrictive requirement than Wholly Within. When a rule specifies Within without the word “Wholly,” partial overlap is sufficient.

A restricted area of the battlefield extending 6” inward from a player’s Entry Edge, as defined by the Deployment Card. Where the Entry Edge does not run the full length of a table edge, the Zone of Influence is marked using Zone of Influence Markers set at the corners of the Entry Edge. Units arriving from Reserves cannot end their deployment Within the opponent’s Zone of Influence. This restriction applies to all forms of arrival - whether by standard deployment, transport, or SUMMON (Part 8.3.3). The Zone of Influence does not affect Units already on the battlefield. It does not restrict movement, block Line of Sight, or interact with any other rule once a Unit has completed its arrival.

Line of Sight determines what a model can see and, by extension, what it can target with attacks and abilities. All Line of Sight checks are resolved from a 2D top-down perspective, looking directly down at the battlefield from above. To determine if a model can see a target, trace an imaginary straight line from any part of the acting model’s base to any part of the target model’s base. Vertical height is never factored into the trace. If the trace does not pass through any Blocking Terrain (any terrain piece with an Effective Size of 1 or greater), the target is Visible. No further checks are required. If the trace passes through Blocking Terrain, the target is not automatically hidden. Apply the Cover rules (Part 7.1.1) to determine whether that terrain actually blocks the Line of Sight: • Full Cover: The terrain’s Effective Size is equal to or greater than the Effective Size of both the attacker and the target. Line of Sight is blocked. • Direct Cover: The trace passes through a terrain piece, and either the attacker or the target is Within 1” of that terrain, provided the terrain’s Effective Size is equal to or greater than the Effective Size of the model that is Within 1”. Line of Sight is blocked. Exception: If both the attacker and the target are Within 1” of the same terrain piece and Within 3” of each other, resolve Line of Sight normally. • Elevation Dead Zone: A model on HIGH GROUND (Size 3+) cannot see a model at GROUND LEVEL that is Within 1” of the base of the same terrain piece, and vice versa. The same Close Quarters exception applies. Each terrain piece is assessed independently. Terrain pieces do not combine their Effective Size or proximity. If no single terrain piece meets the requirements for Full Cover or Direct Cover, Line of Sight is not blocked, regardless of how many terrain pieces the trace passes through. A terrain piece’s footprint is defined by its physical base or outermost edges viewed from above. Gaps, windows, doorways, and open interiors within the footprint do block the Line of Sight unless players agree otherwise during Battlefield Setup (Part 7.1). Flying models ignore the Full Cover rule. Direct Cover and the Elevation Dead Zone still apply. Treat a Flying model’s Effective Size as higher than the Effective Size of any terrain piece on the table (Part 7.1.4). Line of Sight is mutual: if Model A can see Model B, Model B can see Model A through the same trace.

To perform this ability, the controlling player must have sufficient Available Supply. Set one (Name) model in Base-to-Base contact with a model from the active Unit, then remove X models from that Unit from the battlefield. The (Name) model forms a new Unit and cannot be set Within 1” of any Enemy Unit. Place an Activation Marker next to the new Unit; it cannot be Activated for the remainder of the Round.

Every Archon Studio miniature in a player’s army is a model – a single entity (Marine, Zergling, Ultralisk) mounted on its own independent base. All rules apply to the model through its base. The physical miniature above the base is purely for aesthetic purposes.
An army is made up of Units. A Unit is one or more models acting together as a single formation.

Every model stands on a base, and that base is the single most important physical object in the game. It does not matter how a miniature is posed, whether a Zealot is mid-leap or a Hydralisk is rearing back to strike; the rules see only the base. Every measurement, every Line of Sight check, and every question about whether two models are touching or overlapping is resolved by looking at their bases, nothing else.
Tags are keywords printed at the bottom of each Unit Card. They allow rules to target specific types of Units without repeating lengthy definitions.

At any given moment, each player occupies one or more of the following roles. These terms appear throughout the rules and determine who makes decisions, who rolls dice, and who is affected by an ability.

Keywords are written in BOLD CAPS (e.g. SIDEARM, PIERCE, HIDDEN). A keyword always means the same thing, regardless of the Unit in which it appears. Full definitions are in Part 11: Keyword Glossary and Definitions.

Every Special Ability falls into one of three categories. Understanding the difference is essential, as it determines when the ability can be used, whether it requires a conscious decision, and what happens if both players want to act at the same time. Part 10 covers these in full detail; what follows is a working summary.

Active Abilities are deliberate choices, a stim injection, a mode switch, a called shot. They require the Unit to be Activated, and must be triggered immediately before declaring an action or immediately after one fully resolves. A player cannot interrupt an action mid-flow to use one.

Passive Abilities are always active. They represent innate traits, permanent equipment, or biological adaptations that require no decision to activate; they simply function as long as the Unit is on the battlefield.

Reaction Abilities are the battlefield’s reflexes. They fire in response to a specific trigger, such as an incoming attack, an Enemy Charge, or a model being Destroyed, and allow a player to act outside the normal activation sequence. The catch is timing: a Reaction must be declared at the exact moment its trigger occurs. If the moment passes, the opportunity is gone.
The game uses standard six-sided dice (D6).
When a rule calls for a Roll-Off, both players roll 2D6. The higher total wins. Ties are re-rolled until a winner is determined.

Some abilities grant the chance to re-roll, allowing a second attempt when the first result is unfavourable. Pick up the die and roll it again. The new result replaces the original, even if it is worse. Unless stated otherwise, a re-roll applies to a single die. If an ability specifies re-rolling multiple dice, follow its instructions.
Modifiers adjust the Target Number of a roll. Apply all modifiers before rolling.
If a rule says “D3+1”, roll the die and add 1 to the result. This is not a modifier to a Target Number – it generates a value (e.g. 4 Damage instead of 3).
No amount of preparation guarantees a perfect outcome, and no situation is ever truly hopeless. The dice always leave room for the unexpected.

Whenever the rules ask a player to roll against a number, an Armour Roll, a Hit Roll, or an Evade Check, that roll is a Test. Every Test follows the same logic: there is a Target Number, the player rolls, and the result either meets the threshold or it does not.

If a die does not land flat on the playing surface, lodged against terrain, tilted on a base, or off the table entirely, the roll is invalid. Pick it up and roll it again. Players should agree before the game on what constitutes a cocked die. The simplest test: if the result isn’t obvious at a glance, re-roll it.
Coherency is checked at the end of any action that repositions models, including Move, Deploy, Charge, Disengage, Close Ranks, Run, PLACE, and SUMMON.
Every Unit has a Unit Card that provides all the information needed to use it in a game.

No commander goes into combat alone with guns. A creep tumor in a good position, a sensor sweep in reserve, or a psionic storm held back can change a lost battle into a rout. The Tactical Cards are the strategic resources, orders, and doctrines a military leader has available to them, bought before the battle and deployed when they are most needed.
The Faction Card is the foundation of every army. It defines who you are, what doctrine you follow, and what forces you are permitted to bring to the battlefield.

Every conflict has a purpose. A contested line of minerals, a crashed shuttle with vital information, or a Xel’Naga relic glowing with power buried deep beneath the surface. Mission Cards decide what the conflict is about, how long the battle will last, and what must be achieved to win. The mission determines the fight, not the other way round.

The location from which you engage in the battle is as important as what you bring into it. A narrow canyon channels the entire attack into a kill zone. Parallel zones of deployment across open ground give the victory to whoever shoots first. The Deployment Cards determine the war’s geometry, entry points, restricted zones, and the ground that must be taken.
Terrain pieces may block the Line of Sight between models. A terrain piece provides Cover in one of two ways:

If all models of a Unit are standing on HIGH GROUND (Size 3 or larger terrain) with any part of their bases, the Unit becomes eligible to make an Evade Roll against all Ranged Attacks originating from a lower elevation. The attack originates from the lower elevation if at least one model of the attacking Unit isn’t standing on the HIGH GROUND with any part of their base.
Models are Engaged only when all of the following conditions are met:

Tokens represent tangible battlefield assets – Creep Tumors, Corrosive Bile, and Shades. Treat them as Terrain (Size 0) with their own base. Models may move through Tokens, but cannot end movement overlapping them unless specified. Tokens are removed at the end of the Game Round unless stated otherwise. Always measure to the closest base edge of a Token.
Markers are used to keep track of status or game states. Unlike Tokens, they have no physical presence. They do not block Line of Sight or Movement.
When the last model falls, the Unit is Destroyed.

When a Unit arrives from Reserves, that Unit cannot end its arrival during that Activation inside the opponent’s Zone of Influence. This restriction applies to all forms of arrival, whether the Unit enters from an edge, arrives via a Warp Prism, or is summoned. Additionally, a Unit can never end a Deploy action Out of Coherency. If all models cannot be placed legally while maintaining Coherency, the Unit cannot be deployed in that location.
An Unengaged Unit changes its position on the battlefield.

The most challenging manoeuvre a squad will ever make is to pull back under heavy fire. Losing the initiative on a pinned position demands calm discipline, swift action, and enough firepower to keep the pursuers at bay.
The moment boots hit the ground, there is no going back. Timing a deployment correctly can swing an entire flank. Timing it wrong feeds reinforcements into a meat grinder.

Sometimes the best use of a Unit’s activation is not to fight at all. A squad repositioning to claim a Marker next Round, a flanking force closing the gap before a decisive Charge, or a screening Unit pulling back from an exposed position are all valid reasons to give up an entire Assault Phase activation without firing a shot.

Fire is the language of the Assault Phase. A volley of Gauss Rifle rounds tears through a Unit caught crossing open ground. A Hydralisk spine salvo pins down an advancing squad behind a wall. A single Siege Tank shell lands among a cluster of infantry and scatters them. Every ranged weapon on the battlefield has the potential to reshape the fight before the enemy can close the distance, but only if the shot is aimed at the right target, at the right time, with the right weapon.

Every attack is resolved by moving dice through three pools. Dice begin in the Attack Pool, pass through the Armour Pool, and end in the Damage Pool. Dice that survive the entire sequence inflict casualties.
The last few metres are the longest. A charging squad crosses open ground with nothing between them and the Enemy but speed, aggression, and the hope that the dice fall right.

Every battle begins long before the first shot is fired. Players will build an army using two resources: Minerals, which are used for Units and Upgrades, and Vespene Gas, which is used for Tactical Cards.
To ensure that forces are equal, players agree on the Engagement Scale before building an army:
Spend Minerals to recruit Units and purchase Upgrades. The total Mineral cost must not exceed the Engagement Scale limit. Unspent Minerals are lost.
Spend Vespene Gas exclusively on Tactical Cards. It cannot be converted into Minerals. Unspent Vespene Gas is lost.

In multiplayer games (2v2, 3v3, Free-For-All), agree on a Total Mineral Value per team. Teams divide the budget among players as they wish, provided the team’s total remains within the allowed limits. Each player builds their own army independently, selecting their own Faction Card and Tactical Cards. Teammates may choose the same or different Races.
Some Units, such as the Roachling, Point Defence Drone, and Pylon, have no Mineral Cost. These are Summoned Units:
Tournament Override: Organised tournaments may use their own roster visibility rules, which override the default rules below. Always check the Tournament Organiser’s rules pack before attending.
Once the draft is complete and both cards have been chosen, the battlefield is set up in the following order.
All Special Abilities follow the same structure and universal rules. Each ability on a Unit Card or Tactical Card is presented using a consistent format:

faq.q: How do Shields work, and can they be healed?
faq.a: A Unit’s Shield value is added directly to the Hit Points (HP) of its first model. For example, a Zealot (4 HP) with a Shield of 3 gives its first model a total of 7 HP. Lost HP from this combined pool can be healed normally.

faq.q: When exactly is SHIELDED Status lost?
faq.a: SHIELDED Status is lost in either of the following two situations: • The Total Damage assigned to the Unit exceeds its Shield value. For example, a Unit with a Shield of 3 only loses its status after taking 4 or more damage, not 3. Because this is checked after damage is resolved, any abilities that reduce incoming damage before it is assigned can prevent the loss of SHIELDED Status. • The first model in the Unit is removed. Once SHIELDED Status is lost, it cannot be restored by healing.

faq.q: How does non-lethal damage interact with SHIELDED Status?
faq.a: Non-lethal damage is added to the Unit’s Total Damage Pool and removes SHIELDED Status exactly like standard damage.

faq.q: Can a destroyed Unit return to the game?
faq.a: No. Once its last model is removed and a Unit is Destroyed, it cannot return to play. Unless specified otherwise in mission or other rules.

faq.q: How do you check if a Unit is Out of Coherency for the purpose of contesting objectives?
faq.a: Unit Coherency is checked only at the end of a movement. If the Unit passed its last check, it remains in Coherency for objective control, regardless of any casualties suffered since then.

faq.q: Do Gap Clearance rules apply to gaps between models, or only to gaps in or between terrain?
faq.a: They apply to both. A gap is defined as any physical space between terrain pieces or models through which a moving model’s base must pass.

faq.q: Can models be placed on the other side of an enemy unit during a Charge or Close Ranks action, even if there are no gaps?
faq.a: Yes. Coherency Links may pass through Enemy models that your Unit is currently Engaged with. As long as there is open space to place the bases within Coherency, models can be set on the other side of the enemy.

faq.q: Can a Coherency Link pass through terrain, models, and gaps that the Leading Model could move through, or only gaps?
faq.a: It can pass through anything the Leading Model can legally traverse. For example, since Zerg Raptors have special movement rules allowing them to traverse IMPASSABLE TERRAIN, other models in the Unit can trace their Coherency Links directly through that terrain piece to stay connected.

faq.q: Can I place a model onto High Ground from an Access Point using Coherency, or do I need to perform a Move action?
faq.a: You can do so via Coherency, no separate Move action is required. When a Unit resolves a movement, only the nominated Leading Model measures and moves along a physical path. All other models in the Unit are set on the battlefield, and Coherency Links are explicitly allowed to trace through Access Points to connect models across different elevation levels.

faq.q: With the Move or Run actions, can I move 0”?
faq.a: No. A Unit must actually change its position on the battlefield when performing a Move or Run action. If a Unit does not reposition, it is considered to have performed a Hold action instead.

faq.q: Does the Leading Model have to move its maximum distance during a “directly towards” or “directly away” move?
faq.a: Yes. The Leading Model must move the maximum possible distance Directly Towards or Directly Away from the target, as applicable.

faq.q: What happens when a model cannot fit its base on High Ground?
faq.a: Apply the Wobbly Model Syndrome rules. The centre of the model’s base must remain on the High Ground terrain feature, and the base may overhang the edge by the minimum amount necessary to stand.

faq.q: How do Gap Clearance checks work with High Ground, and can you move past a model that is less than an inch from its edge?
faq.a: The edge of a High Ground feature is treated as Impassable Terrain for Gap Clearance purposes. Consequently, any physical space must satisfy the moving model’s Size requirement (1” wide for Size 2 or lower, and 3” wide for Size 3 or larger Units). For example, a Size 3 Siege Tank can drive up a ramp if the gap between the ramp’s edges is at least 3” wide, and it can be placed at the top using the Wobbly Model Syndrome rules if its base cannot fit entirely.

faq.q: Can a Ground Unit move directly between unconnected High Grounds?
faq.a: No. Ground Units can only move between connected High Grounds.

faq.q: Can a model gain Direct Cover by being within 1” of any part of a terrain piece, even if that specific part is not between the model and the attacker, so long as the Line of Sight trace passes through that terrain?
faq.a: Yes. Direct Cover is established as long as the Line of Sight trace passes through a terrain piece and the model is Within 1” of any part of that same terrain piece. It does not matter if the specific section of the terrain Within 1” is the part physically obstructing the trace.

faq.q: Can an objective marker be controlled while it is Deactivated?
faq.a: Yes. Deactivated Mission Markers can still be controlled normally. The rules for determining control apply to all Mission Markers currently on the battlefield, regardless of whether they are flipped to their Activated or Deactivated side.

faq.q: During the Mission and Deployment draft, when both players have the same card, do I remove a specific card or the card name?
faq.a: You block only the specific physical card, not its name. Since players can bring identical cards, removing one physical copy from the table does not discard the duplicate copy, which remains a valid choice.

faq.q: Are the long walls shown in the official map layouts treated as a single terrain feature or as multiple independent terrain pieces?
faq.a: They are treated as multiple independent terrain pieces.

faq.q: Can a Flying or BURROWED Unit claim a Controlled Mission Marker in “Artefact Hunt”?
faq.a: Yes. Rules blocking them from Controlling or Contesting Mission Markers do not prevent them from claiming said markers in the “Artefact Hunt”.

faq.q: If High Ground is touching the edge of the board, can a Unit deploy directly onto it?
faq.a: Yes. Models may deploy directly onto High Ground if the player’s Entry Edge physically touches that terrain feature. All standard deployment requirements still apply, meaning the Unit must be placed legally in Coherency.

faq.q: Does the Omega Network’s ability count as a player’s Entry Edge for rules like Photon Overcharge?
faq.a: Yes. Both the Omega Worm and a Pylon’s base are treated as friendly Entry Edges owned by the player who placed them. • Because they are Friendly Entry Edges, you can trigger abilities like Burrow Ambush from them, and they are immune to enemy denial effects like Photon Overcharge. • Standard forward-deployment cards and transports (e.g., Proxy Barrack, or Warp Prism) do not create Entry Edges. They simply grant a temporary exception to the rules to deploy without one.,

faq.q: Can a Unit deployed through a Pylon as an Entry Edge perform any additional actions or resolve abilities?
faq.a: No. Deploying a Unit this way consumes its entire Activation, which ends immediately upon setup. Once the Unit is placed on the battlefield, you must place an Activation Marker next to it, preventing it from performing any further actions or resolving any other active abilities during that Phase.

faq.q: Does the Omega Network’s ability generate a Zone of Influence (the restricted area extending 6” from a player’s Entry Edge)?
faq.a: No. Zones of Influence are only generated by the primary Entry Edges defined by your Deployment Card and are marked exclusively during battlefield setup.

faq.q: How does deployment work for end-of-round deployment abilities (like Ventral Sacs, Ready For Dust-off, or Warp Conduit) that place a Unit from a marker?
faq.a: Place the leading model in base-to-base contact with the marker, and the remaining models in Unit Coherency completely outside of enemy Engagement Range. If you cannot place the leading model in base-to-base contact with the marker while keeping it outside of enemy Engagement Range, the Unit cannot be deployed, and the ability is wasted.

faq.q: Can a Special Ability be used before deploying a Unit (e. g. , triggering Stimpack to increase its Speed)?
faq.a: No. Abilities do not function while a Unit is in Reserves. Only abilities that explicitly state they work in Reserves (such as “Raiders Roll!”) or those that actually deploy the Unit (like “Armed and Ready” or “Phase Prism”) can be resolved before deployment.

faq.q: What does “Nominated to deploy” mean?
faq.a: This term refers to a Unit actively performing a Deploy Action. Any card effect, special ability, or core game rule that causes a Unit to perform a Deploy Action counts as that Unit being nominated to deploy.

faq.q: Can Units benefit from the Creep speed buff during their Deploy move?
faq.a: No. Units in Reserves cannot use abilities or measure range until they are placed on the battlefield. Because a Unit’s passive abilities do not function while in Reserves and the Unit cannot be “On Creep” before actually entering the board, the Deploy must be resolved using the Unit’s standard Speed characteristic.

faq.q: Do Evade rolls work against Surge?
faq.a: Yes. Evade rolls are resolved against the final Damage Pool, which includes Surge. Surge only bypasses the Armour Roll, moving successful hits directly to the Damage Pool.

faq.q: Can ANTI-EVADE (or any other modifier) ever negate an Evade roll (or any other check) entirely?
faq.a: No. Target numbers can never be modified below 2+ or above 6+. Because abilities like ANTI-EVADE apply modifiers, they can only worsen a check to a maximum of 6+.

faq.q: Can Ranged Attacks destroy target models that are outside of weapon range if they are within Line of Sight?
faq.a: Yes. Casualty removal is restricted only by visibility, not range. Any model in the target Unit that is visible to at least one model in the attacking Unit is eligible to be removed as a casualty, even if that specific model is physically outside of the weapon’s range.

faq.q: When a Unit is engaged, and all of its models are in base-to-base contact, can you perform a Close Ranks action?
faq.a: No. Since the action requires the Leading Model to end their movement closer to the enemy than they started, a Unit where everyone is already in base-to-base contact cannot resolve a Close Ranks action.

faq.q: How are models removed in close combat when fighting multiple enemy Units at once?
faq.a: You must prioritise maintaining engagement with ALL enemy Units. When removing casualties at Priority 2 or 3, you cannot choose a model if its removal would break engagement with a specific enemy Unit, as long as another valid casualty exists in any priority tier.

faq.q: When a Unit has multiple different ranged weapons, must you declare all targets before you begin rolling to hit?
faq.a: No. Targets are declared and resolved one weapon Batch at a time. You select a target for your first weapon type, resolve those attacks completely, and only then declare the target for your next weapon type. Abilities & Tactics Cards

faq.q: How do CP, BM, and PE resources work when paying for special abilities?
faq.a: You must exhaust (flip face-down) one or more Ready cards matching the required resource type to pay the cost. Any excess resources generated are lost and cannot be saved or spent on another ability. For example, exhausting a card that produces 2 CP to pay for a 1 CP ability immediately discards the leftover 1 CP.

faq.q: Is a Unit considered within range of itself for its own abilities?
faq.a: Yes. A Unit is always considered within range of itself unless a rule explicitly states otherwise.

faq.q: Does activating a Tactical Card to use one of its abilities require an active Unit on the battlefield, even if the card doesn’t directly affect that Unit?
faq.a: Yes. An active Unit on the battlefield is always required to resolve a card’s Active Ability.

faq.q: Can a Unit use any number of Active abilities or Tactical Cards during its Activation?
faq.a: Yes. A Unit can resolve any number of differently named Active abilities or Tactical Cards during its Activation, provided you can pay their resource costs. However, Reactions are restricted to one per Activation. Named Active abilities cannot be used more than Once per Round per Unit unless a rule explicitly states otherwise (e.g., a single Marine Unit cannot trigger the “Go! Go! Go!” ability twice in the same Round).

faq.q: When resolving the Marauder’s Concussive Shells reaction, do you need Line of Sight to the charging Enemy Unit or to the Friendly Unit being charged?
faq.a: You only need Line of Sight to the Friendly Unit. Because the ability is measured and targeted toward a Friendly Unit Within 8”, that friendly unit is the subject of the range and visibility check.

faq.q: Can Raptors stack the IMPACT modifiers from Malignant Creep, the Evolution Chamber, and their Adrenal Overload ability?
faq.a: Yes. Because these abilities apply numeric modifiers rather than keywords, they stack. Modifiers from different named sources are cumulative, allowing these three effects to combine for a potential +3 bonus.

faq.q: Can you stack Accelerating Creep with the Queen’s Creep Speed, Wild Mutation, or Roach Glial Reconstitution?
faq.a: Movement modifiers from different named sources stack normally, unless they share the BUFF keyword. Because Accelerating Creep and the Queen’s Creep Speed upgrade apply flat modifiers without using keywords, they stack with other speed bonuses. However, both Wild Mutation and Glial Reconstitution grant the BUFF Speed keyword, meaning they do not stack with each other.

faq.q: Can an opponent place their models on a Faction Indicator (from Ventral Sacs, Ready For Dust-off, or Warp Conduit)?
faq.a: Yes. Opponents can freely move onto and block a Faction Indicator. If the indicator becomes blocked so that you can no longer place a deploying model in base-to-base contact with it, the indicator remains on the field until the End of the Round and is then removed without deploying the Unit.

faq.q: How do you resolve the PLACE (0) effect of Artanis’s Phase Prism ability?
faq.a: Place Artanis directly in base-to-base contact with a model in the selected target Unit.

faq.q: Can damage already assigned to a Unit be removed?
faq.a: Yes. Damage reduction applies to a Unit’s Total Damage (the sum of existing and newly assigned damage). For example, if a Marauder Unit with 2 damage takes 1 additional damage, a Medic’s “Life Support” can remove all 3 damage.

faq.q: Can Roaches move through a Force Field using Tunnelling Claws?
faq.a: No. Tunnelling Claws only allow a Unit to move through enemy Units, not Terrain. Since a Force Field is classified as Terrain, it cannot be bypassed or moved through using this ability.

faq.q: Can a Size 3 Unit be PLACED into a Force Field to automatically remove it?
faq.a: No. Because a PLACE effect is not a movement, it cannot remove a Force Field.

faq.q: Can Raptors move across Force Fields, since they can normally bypass terrain?
faq.a: No. Force Fields explicitly forbid Units of Size 2 or less from moving across them. Because Raptors are Size 1, they cannot ignore this specific terrain restriction.

faq.q: When is ON CREEP checked for the movement bonus from Accelerating Creep?
faq.a: At the start of the movement. If a Unit is ON CREEP when it begins its movement, it gains the bonus for the entire move, even if it leaves Creep during that movement.

faq.q: Can you use the Advanced Training reaction from the Academy if the card is already exhausted?
faq.a: No. Once a Tactical Card is Exhausted, none of its printed abilities can be resolved or used until the card is Refreshed during the Phase 4 Cleanup.

faq.q: Can you resolve Reaction Abilities outside of an activation?
faq.a: Yes. Reactions can be resolved at any time their specific trigger conditions are met, regardless of whether a Unit is currently activated. • Outside of activations, you are restricted to resolving only one Reaction per trigger (provided the participating Unit has not already used that reaction this round). • If both players attempt to react to the same trigger outside of an activation, the holder of the First Player Marker resolves theirs first.

faq.q: What counts as targeting a Structure?
faq.a: Abilities can affect a Structure if they target an area or the Unit itself rather than a specific individual model. Structures are only excluded from an ability’s effects if that ability’s targeting requirements, keywords, or restrictions rule them out.

faq.q: What is the difference between “select” and “target”?
faq.a: There is no mechanical or rules distinction between these two terms. They are treated as synonyms.

faq.q: Can an Adept Unit use Psionic Transfer to “teleport” while carrying a claimed Mission Marker in the “Artefact Hunt” mission?
faq.a: No.

faq.q: Does PINPOINT allow a Unit to ignore its own engagement and shoot at outside targets, or does it only allow targeting an engaged enemy?
faq.a: It only allows shooting into combat, not shooting out of it. The keyword overrides the targeting restriction on the target Unit, allowing models to shoot at Engaged enemies.

faq.q: Can I remove a Creep Token by using the PLACE keyword?
faq.a: No. Creep Removal only triggers when an enemy Unit ends a Move, Deploy, Run, Charge, or Disengage action within 1” of a Creep Tumor. As PLACE is neither of those, ending a PLACE movement near a Creep Tumor does not remove it.

faq.q: To benefit from the LOCKED IN keyword, must the attacking model be stationary, or does the target need to have Stationary Status?
faq.a: The target must have the Stationary Status.

faq.q: How does Indirect Fire work against a target Unit when only some of its models are visible?
faq.a: The target Unit does not gain an Evade roll, and non-visible models can still be removed as casualties. Because at least one model is visible, the target Unit itself is considered to be within Line of Sight, meaning it does not qualify for the Evade roll granted to out-of-sight targets.

faq.q: Since HIDDEN Units cannot be targeted from more than 4” away, how can “detection” abilities (such as Scanner Sweep, Oversight Mode, or Surveillance) affect them at a 6” range?
faq.a: These abilities target a location on the battlefield rather than the Units themselves. They place a Faction Indicator to create a 6” area of effect. Because the ability does not select the Unit as a target, it bypasses the 4” targeting restriction.

faq.q: When are abilities or effects with a “while within” condition checked?
faq.a: These effects are checked at the start and the end of any action or ability during the game round. If a Unit is within the specified range and meets all other requirements, the effect applies immediately.

faq.q: Can a Reaction ability with the REPEATABLE keyword be used multiple times during the same Activation?
faq.a: No. The standard limit of one Reaction per Activation still applies. While REPEATABLE allows the ability to be used across different Activations during the round, it cannot be used multiple times in the same Activation. For triggers that occur outside of an Activation entirely, the ability can only be used once per trigger.

faq.q: Do keywords like PRECISION, SURGE, or CRITICAL HIT apply to individual models, or do they apply to the entire Unit?
faq.a: They apply to the weapon Batch (the collective dice pool generated by the Unit’s attack) rather than to individual models. Models in a Unit using the same weapon profile combine their Rate of Attack (RoA) dice into a single pool, and these keywords act on the dice within that pool. Individual models are tracked separately only to determine Range, visibility, and specific per- model roll modifiers (such as the -1 Hit penalty for Long Range).

faq.q: How do abilities like PRECISION work when splitting attacks in combat against multiple enemy Units?
faq.a: Splitting attacks is resolved as a single Batch, allowing you to allocate keyword effects as they are resolved. Because the attacks against both Units occur simultaneously, you can choose to apply keywords like PRECISION entirely to one target’s pool or split them across both pools.

faq.q: Does morphing a Unit award Victory Points (VPs) to the opponent if the original Unit’s Supply Value is reduced?
faq.a: Yes. Anytime a Unit’s Current Supply Value is reduced, including during a Morph, the opponent gains Victory Points (VPs) equal to the amount of Supply lost.

faq.q: Does a MORPHED Unit award Victory Points (VPs) to the opponent when the Units’ Supply Value is reduced?
faq.a: Yes. A MORPHED Unit awards Victory Points (VPs) exactly like any other Unit on the battlefield, equal to the amount of Supply lost.

faq.q: If a Specialist model (like an AGG-12 Marine) is removed, can you keep the weapon in play by replacing another model that doesn’t have it?
faq.a: No. You cannot transfer Specialist models to other models or replace a model without the weapon to keep the Specialist.

faq.q: How do Blast Template abilities (like Psionic Storm or Plague) resolve without a physical “Primary Target” to establish a Target Point, Elevation Level, or Combat Tags?
faq.a: You resolve them using the template rules with the following key adaptations: • The Unit executing the ability is treated as the Attacking Model.

faq.q: Does the Spillover requirement to “share the same Combat Tag as the Primary target” prevent a template from spilling over to models with different tags (e.g., from Light Zerglings to Armoured Roaches), or is it only meant to check Ground vs. Flying status?
faq.a: Spillover targets only need to share at least one Combat Tag and match the elevation level of the Primary target. Since Zerglings and Roaches both share the Ground Combat Tags, a template can spill over between them if they are on the same elevation. Mutalisks cannot be affected by Ground-level templates even though they share the Biological tag, because Flying Units do not occupy a standard Elevation Level for template purposes.

faq.q: How does Guardian Shield interact with Spillover?
faq.a: Because Spillover hits are resolved as separate attack batches, the Guardian Shield modifier applies to each batch individually. Any Ranged Attack (including both the main target and any Spillover batches) targeting a friendly Unit affected by the Guardian Shield is made with 1 fewer die in its Attack Pool.

faq.q: How do keywords such as PRECISION (X) or CRITICAL HIT (X) interact with Spillover?
faq.a: Weapon keywords apply exclusively to the Attack Pool generated against the Main Target. They do not carry over to Spillover batches, which are resolved as separate, basic attack batches without modifiers.
